summary:
Albania does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or gender expression. Homosexuality carried a ten-year prison sentence until 1995. The operative instrument since 4 February 2010 is a comprehensive anti-discrimination law that covers sexual orientation in employment, goods and services, education, housing and health care, and that was expanded in October 2020 to prohibit discrimination on the grounds of sex characteristics and HIV status.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised in any form, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex couples. Since Parliament amended the criminal code on 4 May 2013, hate-motivated offences based on sexual orientation and gender identity are treated on a par with offences motivated by race, ethnicity, religion or disability. The package adopted the same day also penalised dissemination of homophobic information by any means, including the internet, with a fine and up to two years' imprisonment.

No provision restricting bathrooms or other facilities appears anywhere in the sources reviewed, and nothing indicates trans-specific screening at the border or on arrival. The realistic exposure for a trans visitor is social and medical rather than statutory. Rainbowphilia logged ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people during 2023, and hostility is reported as sharper outside Tirana and in more conservative rural areas. A 2022 nationwide questionnaire found that only 9.3% of Albanians would accept an LGBT person as a family doctor, which bears on routine care-seeking. Tirana hosts an annual Pride.

The UN Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity visited Albania from 1 to 12 July 2024, and the resulting report (A/HRC/59/43/Add.1, 17 June 2025) is the current international-review baseline for the country's conditions.
tangentialFactors:
Political rhetoric has run well ahead of the legal position. In 2009 the then Prime Minister Sali Berisha voiced support for same-sex marriage and framed the 2010 anti-discrimination law as EU-integration driven; the law that passed omitted any marriage provision. Ten years later, in July 2021, Democratic Party MP Luçiano Boçi attacked LGBT campaigning in high schools as extra-curricular groups with a suspicious and revolting agenda, while MP Nard Ndoka used Facebook to brand the government LGBT and to accuse it of pushing LGBT values in schools. Both episodes belong to the same week of parliamentary and opposition messaging.

Earlier, in October 2011, the Anti-Discrimination Commissioner reprimanded ruling Democratic Party MP Tritian Shehu for telling parliament that homosexuality is a disease and should be treated with hormones, warning him to avoid remarks that create an atmosphere of tension toward the LGBT community. In 2016, under pressure from faith-based leaders, members of parliament removed sexual orientation and gender identity from Article 18 of the Constitution at the last moment, contrary to prior promises; an LGBTI advocacy organisation condemned the removal on 20 July 2016. A government National Action Plan for LGBTI adopted in June 2016 to address bullying and discrimination in primary and secondary education drew strong political opposition on similar grounds.
localsOnly:
Residents live under machinery that exists on paper and performs unevenly. The Commissioner for Protection from Discrimination was slow to act on the Shehu remarks, reprimanding him only on 30 September 2011, and LGBT groups had by then lost trust in the body over bureaucratically impeded investigations; by December 2012 only one of nine LGBT-linked cases had been concluded. In 2023 the same office mediated complaints filed over screenings of the film 'Strange World', ruling in favour of the complainants in one case.

Community organisations deliver services the state does not. Support schemes have included food packages for trans sex workers and for people living with HIV. A National LGBTI Action Plan runs from 2021 to 2027, and observers record that implementation falls short of the commitments made. Attitudinal data are consistently hostile: a 2010 Gallup Balkan Monitor survey found 56.1% of Albanians saying homosexuals should not show their preferences in public and 56.2% saying they should not hold public posts such as teacher; a 2015 survey of 16-to-27-year-olds found 55% would not want homosexual neighbours; a 2016 study associated homophobia among university students with being male, politically conservative and religious.

Visibility efforts continue despite that climate. Pro LGBT launched the news portal historiaime.al in 2012, and the first Miss Trans Albania pageant was held in Tirana in 2014.
outOfScopeNotes:
Legal gender recognition is unresolved. In April 2018 the People's Advocate Erinda Ballanca pledged to support the right to legally change one's gender, but no source reviewed states whether a procedure exists, what it requires, or how identity documents are handled for trans residents or visitors. A trans visitor cannot confirm from this inventory what marker or name change is achievable on an Albanian document.

Several further points are unresolved rather than settled. No source documents enforcement of the 2013 hate-crime provision in any individual case, and none documents enforcement of the measure penalising dissemination of homophobic information. The current text of Article 18 of the Constitution after the 2016 removal is not reproduced in any source here. The specific recommendations made to Albania in the 2025 UN report are not itemised in the inventory. The most recent ILGA-Europe country review available covers 2023, so conditions in 2024 and 2025 are not sourced. Whether medical staff are legally required to treat trans patients, as distinct from the recorded attitude data, is not stated.
